content.thinking:
I'm noticing a timing discrepancy: the flag change events appear to register after 07:49, yet error logs and flag evaluations already show problems starting around 07:44, with partial and then full activation by 07:45. That means the recorded change timestamp comes after the actual onset of issues, which seems worth digging into further.

Even more puzzling, the revert at 07:49:20 doesn't seem to have resolved the errors—flag=on evaluations continue through 07:50 and 07:51, well after the revert should have taken effect, and errors persist until the revert itself gets undone at 07:51:30. So either the revert didn't actually propagate to evaluation, or there's something else at play, which leaves the real cause still unclear.

Piecing the chain together: account page requests fail with ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, tied to the monthly-spend-feature flag being evaluated as on starting around 07:44 and fully on shortly after. The admin toggle timestamp at 07:49:09 doesn't cleanly match the 07:44 onset, which is a gap I need to flag as an assumption rather than treat as settled.

Contributing factors stand out: there was no canary or guard on the flag rollout, and the revert didn't actually work though it's unclear why — that needs further investigation into how flag evaluation propagates. I also notice memory of a prior incident (T15/T38) where the same revert failed, but that memory wasn't used to deprioritize the fix attempt before acting at T18, which points to a process gap in using prior-incident knowledge proactively.

There's also a timestamp discrepancy worth flagging — the change event appears dated after onset, which makes flag-audit timestamps unreliable for detection purposes, and the alert itself lagged onset by several minutes, suggesting detection latency is a contributing factor too.

Now I'm drafting the numbered action items: fixing the division-by-zero bug and adding a zero-case test, implementing staged rollout with an automatic error-rate guard for flags, and investigating why turning the flag off didn't actually stop the issue.

I should add a process item requiring teams to consult outcomes from past incidents before choosing a mitigation, plus a detection item around faster error-rate alerting correlated with flag changes and reconciling event timestamps. For the executive summary, I need to be careful to avoid writing specific clock times or exact figures like line numbers, using placeholders like duration or began instead.

action_items.item: Fix the division by zero in spend_summary.py, handling the empty or zero-denominator case, and add a regression test that covers it before the flag is enabled again.
Roll this flag and similar flags out in stages, with an automatic rollback if the error rate of the gated service rises above baseline.

Find out why turning monthly-spend-feature off did not stop the errors. Check whether the provider's off state reaches the replicas, whether evaluations are cached, and whether the rollout percentage is stuck. Then add a post-revert check that flag evaluations in the logs really changed.
Make Argus consult the outcomes of earlier similar incidents before choosing a mitigation, and avoid or rank last any action that already failed on a matching incident.
Alert sooner on a sharp error-rate rise on io-shop, and fix the flag change audit so each change is recorded once with the time it took effect.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, and the service had not recovered when metrics were last read.

The failing requests raised a ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) in spend_summary.py, the monthly spend summary code on the account page. Latency stayed flat, so these were fast failures rather than overload.
That code path was being executed because the feature flag monthly-spend-feature was evaluating as on. Evaluations moved from mostly off to mostly on around the onset and stayed on afterward.

The flag was enabled by an admin and exposed the spend-summary code to nearly all traffic with no gradual rollout or automatic guard that would stop on a rising error rate. The change record is dated after the onset, so its timing does not line up cleanly with the log evidence.

Switching the flag off did not bring the service back, and flag-on evaluations and the division errors still appeared in the logs afterward. The record cannot say why: the revert may not have taken effect, or another condition keeps the faulty path active. The chain stops here for lack of evidence.

contributing_factors.factor: The code path behind the flag had a division by zero that was not caught by tests or review before the flag was enabled in production.
The flag went to nearly all traffic quickly, with no staged rollout or automatic rollback on error rate.
The revert of the flag did not stop the errors and the reason is unknown. It is unclear whether flag-off propagates to the service, or whether a stuck rollout or cached evaluation exists.
Argus chose the flag revert even though memory held an earlier similar incident where the same action had not helped. The record only down-ranked it after the attempt failed.
The alert fired several minutes after the onset. The change audit trail is dated after the onset, with duplicate entries, which makes it hard to correlate the flag change with the errors.

input.executive_summary: Starting at {began}, a large share of shoppers' account page requests failed. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service had not recovered when metrics were last read, so it was down for at least {duration}. Errors coincided with the rollout of a new monthly-spend feature, whose code divides by zero. Argus switched the feature flag off, but errors continued, so it judged the action refuted and put the flag back as it had been. It then escalated to humans for lack of evidence, after {held}. The service was not shown to be healthy again, and the reason the rollback did not help is still unknown.

got_lucky: The errors were fast failures with flat latency and confined to the account page, so they did not appear to overload the service or spread to other pages.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, found the flag change and the matching ZeroDivisionError log line quickly, and acted at once.
When the revert did not help, Argus judged it refuted, restored the flag to its earlier state and escalated rather than looping on the same fix.
went_wrong: The mitigation tried had already failed on a similar earlier incident, and it was only de-prioritised after it failed again.
The service was not shown to be healthy at the end, and the escalation has no confirmed explanation for why the revert failed.
The change record's timestamps and duplicate entries do not match the onset seen in the metrics and logs.

input.root_cause: The account-page spend-summary code path, which is enabled by the feature flag monthly-spend-feature, raises a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py, and it was exposed to nearly all traffic when the flag went on. Why switching the flag back off did not stop the errors is not established, so the fault is only partly explained.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
